descriptor.note: Copied by a script from the data inside the VCAA Science curriculum page on 10 November 2026, not typed from memory.
descriptor.text: light can be produced from many sources; light travels in a straight path, can form shadows, and can be absorbed, transmitted, reflected or refracted by objects
descriptor.attribution: Victorian Curriculum Foundation to Level 10 content is © VCAA, licensed CC BY-NC 3.0 Australia. The official curriculum is on the VCAA website.

paraphrase.note: My reading of the description and its achievement standard. The achievement standard wording was checked on the VCAA page: students identify sources of light and model different pathways of light to explain what they observe.
paraphrase.text: Students build one working model of light and use it to explain things they can see. Light comes out of a source, travels in straight lines until it meets something, and then one or more of four things happens to it. The assessable skill is not naming the four words. It is drawing or modelling the path the light takes, from the source to the object (and on to the eye), to explain a shadow, a reflection or a bent-looking pencil.
asks_for: Light comes from sources, and there are many kinds, natural and made.
Light travels in straight lines out from its source.
A shadow forms where an object blocks the light, which follows from straight-line travel.

When light meets an object it can be absorbed, transmitted (let through), reflected (bounced off) or refracted (change direction as it passes into a different transparent material). Most objects do more than one of these.
not_asking: The wave or particle nature of light, or the electromagnetic spectrum. That is Levels 9 and 10 (VC2S10U14).
The law of reflection with measured angles, lenses, or how the eye works inside.
Colour theory. One elaboration has students see the rainbow effect from a prism or water droplets, but only as an observation of refraction.

key_questions.note: The natural and artificial examples follow a VCAA elaboration (glow-worms, the Sun and stars; light bulbs and candles).
key_questions.question: Where does light come from?
know: A light source makes its own light: the Sun, stars, a flame, a globe, a screen, a glow-worm.
Sources can be natural or made by people.
Most things we see are not sources. The Moon, a mirror and a white wall only send on light that came from a source.
understand: Without a source there is no light, and in complete darkness nothing can be seen.
We see objects that are not sources because light from a source reflects off them.
do: Sort objects into light sources and things that only reflect light, and justify the tricky ones (the Moon, a mirror, reflective tape).

key_questions.question: How does light travel?
know: Light travels in straight lines, outward from the source in all directions.
It keeps going until it meets something.
A ray is a line with an arrow that we draw to show the path of light.
understand: Light is in the space between the source and the place it lights up, even when we cannot see a beam.
A ray is a model, a drawing of a path. It is not a thing you could pick up.
do: Predict where light will land (for example through holes that are, or are not, lined up) and test it.
Draw light paths as straight arrows that start at the source.

key_questions.note: Shadow length and the position of the Sun come from a VCAA elaboration (sundials and shadow puppets).
key_questions.question: How is a shadow made, and what changes it?
know: A shadow is a place the light does not reach because an object is in the way.
A shadow needs three things: a source, an object that blocks light, and a surface behind it.
A shadow gets bigger when the object moves closer to the source, and longer when the source is lower (the Sun early and late in the day).
understand: Shadows are evidence that light travels in straight lines: it cannot curve around the object.
A shadow is an absence of light, not a thing the object sends out.
do: Predict, test and measure how a shadow changes when one thing is changed.
Explain a shadow with a ray diagram: source, object, surface, and the rays that are blocked.

key_questions.note: The three outcomes for light meeting an object, and the meanings of opaque, translucent and transparent, were checked against the IOPSpark narrative. The rest is my judgement.
key_questions.question: What can happen when light meets an object?
know: Light can be transmitted (pass through), reflected (bounce off) or absorbed (taken in by the object).
Transparent objects let almost all light through, translucent objects let some through, and opaque objects let none through.
Most objects do a mix: a window transmits most light and still reflects some.
understand: Every object we can see is reflecting some light, not only mirrors and shiny things.
We see an object when light from it enters our eyes: source, then object, then eye.
do: Test everyday materials with a torch and classify what each mostly does to light.
Model the path of light that lets someone see an object, with arrows pointing the right way.

key_questions.note: The prism and water droplet examples follow a VCAA elaboration. The level of explanation expected is my judgement.
key_questions.question: Why do things look bent or out of place through water or glass?
know: Refraction is light changing direction as it passes from one transparent material into another, such as from water into air.
The light travels in a straight line on each side. The change of direction happens at the boundary.
understand: The pencil is not bent. The light from it has changed direction on the way to our eyes, so we see it in a different place.
Refraction through a prism or water droplets can spread light into a rainbow.
do: Observe and describe refraction (a pencil in water, a coin that reappears) and draw the light changing direction at the surface.
Tell reflection and refraction apart in everyday examples.

vocabulary.note: The choice of words and tiers is my judgement. Words marked as in the description were checked against the VCAA wording. Meanings are mine, written for students, apart from transparent, translucent and opaque, which match the IOPSpark narrative.

academic.meaning: To move from one place to another.
The outside or top layer of something.
The way something is pointing or moving.
A drawing or object that shows how something works.
To say what you think will happen, with a reason.
Found in nature, or made by people.

science.meaning: Something that makes its own light.
A straight line with an arrow that shows the path of light.
To take light in, so it does not pass through or bounce off.
To bounce light off a surface.
To change the direction of light as it passes into a different transparent material.
Lets almost all light through, so you can see clearly through it.
Lets some light through, but you cannot see clearly through it.

misconceptions.idea: Light lights up the room, and that is enough for seeing. It does not have to go into my eyes.
misconceptions.science: We only see something when light from it enters our eyes.
misconceptions.respond: Ask students to draw how a person sees a book in a lit room, then look for who has any line reaching the eye.
research: Andersson and Kärrqvist (1983), Swedish students aged 12 to 15
Eaton, Anderson and Smith (1983), fifth-grade students

misconceptions.note: The Research-2-Practice summary also states that primary pupils do not understand how we see objects, citing Fetherstonhaugh (1990) and Osborne et al. (1990).
misconceptions.idea: Seeing goes from the eye to the object: I look at it, so something travels out from my eyes. Some students draw light going from the source to the eye and then on to the object.
misconceptions.science: Light travels from the source to the object, reflects off it, and then enters the eye. Nothing travels out of the eye.
misconceptions.respond: Check the direction of the arrows on every diagram. A model with string or ribbon from torch to object to eye makes the order concrete.

misconceptions.idea: Light is in the bright places (the lamp and the patch it lights up) but not in the space between. Or light simply fills a room and is just there, not coming from anywhere.
misconceptions.science: Light is travelling through all the space between the source and whatever it lights, in straight lines, even where we cannot see a beam.
misconceptions.respond: Put a sheet of paper at different points between a torch and the wall. The paper lights up everywhere along the path.

misconceptions.idea: A shadow is a thing that belongs to the object: a dark reflection or a copy of its shape, so it is always the same shape as the object. Younger children mix up shadow and reflection.
misconceptions.science: A shadow is where light is missing because the object blocked it. Its shape and size change with the position of the source, the object and the surface.
misconceptions.respond: Have students predict the shadow of one object from three torch positions before they test it, then explain the surprise.

misconceptions.idea: Light bounces off mirrors and shiny things, but not off ordinary objects like paper, a jumper or a face.
misconceptions.science: Every object we can see reflects some light. A mirror reflects it in an orderly way. A rough or dull surface scatters it in all directions.
misconceptions.respond: In a dim room, shine a torch on white paper held near a wall and watch the wall get brighter.
research: Eaton, Anderson and Smith (1983), fifth-grade students

misconceptions.note: Not checked against research. IOPSpark lists a related entry (students believing light can change direction or curve with nothing acting on it) that I saw by title only and did not read.
misconceptions.idea: In refraction the water bends the pencil, or light curves as it goes through the water.
misconceptions.science: The pencil stays straight and so does the light on each side of the surface. The light changes direction once, at the boundary between water and air.
misconceptions.respond: Draw the ray as two straight pieces with one corner at the water surface.

misconceptions.note: Widely reported by teachers, but I did not check it against a source.
misconceptions.idea: The Moon is a light source, because it shines at night.
misconceptions.science: The Moon makes no light. We see it because it reflects light from the Sun.
misconceptions.respond: Include the Moon in the sources sorting task and let students argue it out.

inquiry.note: The VCAA elaboration for this code uses a light example: predicting whether an arrangement of mirrors will let you see around a corner.
inquiry.how: Students make a reasoned prediction before each test: where the shadow will fall, whether the light will get through, whether the mirrors will let them see around the corner.

inquiry.note: The code and its wording were checked on the VCAA page. The link to light is my judgement.
inquiry.how: Shadow size is a clean fair test: change one thing (distance from torch to object), measure one thing (shadow height) and keep the rest the same.

inquiry.note: The VCAA elaboration for this code uses a light example: comparing the precision of class data on the length of shadows at different times of day.
inquiry.how: Students measure shadow lengths with a ruler, repeat the measurement and compare how close the class results are.

inquiry.note: The code and its wording were checked on the VCAA page. The link is my judgement, supported by the achievement standard, which asks students to model pathways of light.
inquiry.how: Ray diagrams are the model. Students draw and annotate light paths to explain what they saw, and can graph shadow height against distance.

human_endeavour.note: The VCAA lists this as an elaboration of VC2S6U08 itself. It gives no detail beyond the sentence, so the specifics (which Peoples, which materials, how the practice is taught) are not verified here. Find a named local or published First Nations source before teaching it, and do not present it as one practice shared by all Peoples.
human_endeavour.hook: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples' knowledge of light: allowing for refraction when spearfishing (the fish is not where it appears to be), shimmering body paint, and reflection as a reason for the materials chosen for housing.

human_endeavour.note: From a VCAA elaboration of VC2S6H02. A related elaboration of VC2S6U01 covers the effect of urban lighting on nocturnal and migratory animals. The design challenge is my suggestion.
human_endeavour.hook: Light pollution: how communities use what they know about light to reduce it, with shielded streetlights that point down, lights that switch off automatically and motion sensors. A natural design challenge: shape a shade so light goes only where it is needed.

human_endeavour.note: The code and its wording (scientific knowledge changes over time and builds on the work of others) were checked on the VCAA page. The historical example is from my general knowledge and has not been checked against a source.
human_endeavour.hook: How ideas about seeing changed. Many early thinkers believed sight came out of the eyes. About a thousand years ago the scholar Ibn al-Haytham used experiments to argue that we see because light enters the eye. Students often hold the older idea, so the history meets them where they are.

below.summary: There is no light content description at Foundation to Level 2 or at Levels 3 and 4. I searched all 55 Science content descriptions from Foundation to Level 6: VC2S6U08 is the first to teach light. Students may arrive with everyday ideas only.
Patterns in the changing positions of the Sun, Moon, planets and stars. The nearest earlier experience of shadows: an elaboration of VC2S2I02 has students measure shadows with chalk and string.
Sources of heat energy and heat moving from one object to another. The previous Physical sciences description about a form of energy, and the first use of the idea of a source.

same.summary: The Sun and planets, and how the positions of Earth and the Sun explain day and night. Shares the Sun as a light source and the changing length of shadows.
Electrical circuits, conductors and insulators. An elaboration has circuits transforming electrical energy into heat, light and sound, so a globe or LED is a made light source.

above.summary: There is no content description about light itself at Levels 7 and 8. The next direct treatment is at Levels 9 and 10.
Models of Earth, the Sun and the Moon to explain eclipses, seasons and tides. Uses shadows and straight-line travel on a much bigger scale.
Forms of energy, and energy transfers including radiation. Light becomes one case of energy being transferred.
Wave and particle models of energy transfer, and the properties of electromagnetic and mechanical waves. This is where light is explained, rather than described.

anchors.note: A standard classroom demonstration, written from my own knowledge. Not tried in the STEAM room.
anchors.title: Three cards and a torch
anchors.phenomenon: Light from a torch gets through three cards with holes only when the holes are in one straight line. Move one card a little and the spot on the wall disappears.
anchors.students_do: Predict, then line up the cards so the light reaches the wall. Thread a string through the holes and pull it tight to show the path. Draw the ray.
materials: Three pieces of card with a hole punched in the same place
A small torch or a phone torch (most iPads have no torch)
Blu Tack or pegs to stand the cards up
anchors.shows: Light travels in a straight path.
anchors.caution: No laser pointers, and no torches shone at eyes.

anchors.note: A standard investigation, written from my own knowledge. Not tried in the STEAM room.
anchors.title: Grow the shadow
anchors.phenomenon: The same small object makes a huge shadow or a small one, depending only on how far it is from the torch.
anchors.students_do: Predict what will happen to the shadow as the object moves towards the torch. Measure the shadow height at three or four distances, record it in a table, and explain it with a ray diagram.
materials: A small torch or a phone torch (most iPads have no torch)
A small opaque object such as a LEGO figure or a glue stick
White paper on a wall or a box as a screen
anchors.shows: Shadows form where an object blocks light, and their size follows from light travelling in straight lines.
anchors.caution: The room needs to be dim. If it cannot be darkened, work inside a large box or under a table. Use one torch per group: two sources make two overlapping shadows.

anchors.note: Standard demonstrations, written from my own knowledge. Not tried in the STEAM room.
anchors.title: What does light do here? Torch test and the coin that comes back
anchors.phenomenon: The same torch beam passes through a plastic sleeve, glows through baking paper, bounces off foil onto the ceiling and stops at black card. Then a coin hidden below the rim of a cup comes into view when water is poured in, without anyone moving.
anchors.students_do: Test each material and record what it mostly does to light: transmit, reflect or absorb. Then set up the coin so it is just out of sight, add water slowly, and draw where the light changes direction.
materials: A small torch or a phone torch (most iPads have no torch)
Foil, baking paper, a clear plastic sleeve, white paper and black card
An opaque cup, a coin and a jug of water
A pencil and a clear cup of water for the bent pencil
anchors.shows: Light can be absorbed, transmitted, reflected or refracted by objects.
anchors.caution: Keep water away from the iPads. This is two short stations, so it suits a rotation.

pitfalls.note: Based on the achievement standard, which asks students to model pathways of light to explain what they observe.
pitfalls.pitfall: Stopping at vocabulary: sorting objects into transparent, translucent and opaque and calling the description done.
pitfalls.instead: Make the ray diagram the main product of every lesson. Each activity ends with students drawing the light path and using it to explain what happened.

pitfalls.note: The description does not mention seeing or the eye, but the research on student ideas (see Misconceptions) centres on it.
pitfalls.pitfall: Leaving the eye out of diagrams, or accepting arrows that point from the eye to the object.
pitfalls.instead: Always finish the path at an eye, and check the arrows: source, then object, then eye.

pitfalls.pitfall: Teaching reflection only with mirrors, which confirms the idea that ordinary objects do not reflect light.
pitfalls.instead: Say early and often that everything we can see is reflecting light. Use white paper and coloured card as reflectors as well as mirrors.

pitfalls.note: The Best Evidence Science Teaching notes report (citing Driver et al., 1994) that students can think of rays as wires of light or as roads from A to B.
pitfalls.pitfall: Talking about rays as if they are real things in the air.
pitfalls.instead: Call the ray a drawing of the path light takes, and say that we draw only a few of the countless paths.

pitfalls.pitfall: Saying only that refraction bends light, which students hear as light curving or the object bending.
pitfalls.instead: Say that light changes direction at the surface where two transparent materials meet, and is straight on both sides.

pitfalls.pitfall: Running shadow puppets or mirror mazes as a fun activity with no prediction and no explanation.
pitfalls.instead: Keep the fun, and wrap it in predict, test, explain: students commit to a prediction first and draw the reason after.

pitfalls.pitfall: A room that is too bright or has several light sources, so shadows are faint, double or fuzzy and the evidence is unclear.
pitfalls.instead: Use one small bright source per group and the dimmest space available: a box, a cupboard corner or under a table.

pitfalls.pitfall: Over-reaching into angles of reflection, lenses, colour mixing or waves because students ask.
pitfalls.instead: Park those questions as wonderings. The description needs a secure straight-line model first, and the rest comes at Levels 9 and 10.

unverified: I could not read the original research studies. Journal sites and the STEM Learning library blocked access, so every misconception marked verified rests on a published research summary that I did read (IOPSpark, Best Evidence Science Teaching, Research-2-Practice) and that names the studies. The studies themselves are listed as not read.
The two draft misconceptions (refraction, and the Moon as a light source) are not backed by a source I read.
The First Nations examples are confirmed only as far as the VCAA's one-sentence elaboration. I did not find or check a First Nations source for the detail.
The Ibn al-Haytham example is from general knowledge and was not checked.
The anchor experiences have not been trialled in the STEAM room, and I did not check whether the room can be made dim enough.
I did not find Australian research on Year 5 and 6 students' ideas about refraction.
